newsitem.title: NEPAL: Sister Nirmala's family lauds her sacrifices.
newsitem.headline: Sister Nirmala's family lauds her sacrifices.

text.p: Relatives of Sister Nirmala expressed pride and joy on Thursday over her selection to head Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity order and said she deserved the honour because of her sacrifices.
"We are very happy," Rajendra Prasad Joshi, the nun's younger brother told Reuters in the Nepali capital Kathmandu.
Devout Hindus, the Joshis originally came from a village in the Syangja region in western Nepal. Most of them still live in Nepal, the world's only Hindu kingdom.
Sister Nirmala's deceased father, Mahananda Joshi, served in the military police in the northern Indian state of Bihar, where Mother Teresa's successor was born.
Rajendra Prasad Joshi, said Nirmala, the eldest of eight sisters and two brothers, deserved to be selected.

"She was a deserving candidate because of her own performance and sacrifice," said her 42-year-old brother, who lives in the Bihari town of Dhanbad where most of the children were born. Sister Nirmala is 63. Rajendra, who still lives in Dhanbad teaching psychology, was in the Nepali capital visiting relatives.
Sister Nirmala's other brother, Surendra Prasad Joshi, is a college teacher and lives in Kathmandu. One of her sisters is dead and the six others live in Nepal.
Nirmala's parents, high-caste Hindu Brahmins, did not oppose her joining the Missionaries of Charity, family members said. One of her sisters has joined another Roman Catholic order.

Relatives said that during trips to Kathmandu, Sister Nirmala, who holds a master's degree in political science, has often visited the Lord Pashupatinath temple, a sacred Hindu shrine which non-Hindus are not allowed to enter.
She would offer prayers from the gate of the temple.

"She told us that all gods were equal and worshipped them equally," said Nina Joshi, Sister Nirmala's niece. "My aunt liked to serve the poor. That is why she became a nun and is very polite to everyone."
